name: Threat Assessment
title: Threat Assessment
answer: Threat assessment is the process a school uses when a student may pose a danger to others, in which a trained team gathers information, judges how serious the concern is and decides on a response. AI has a narrow supporting role here, limited to documentation through approved tools, because the decisions themselves shape a student's education, safety and future and must be made by people. The idea matters because a machine that produces a risk judgment first can pull a team toward a conclusion it might not otherwise have reached.

sections.body: Threat assessment is the structured process schools follow when a student may present a danger to others. A trained team collects information, weighs the level of concern, and settles on a response. The problem it addresses is that these judgments carry heavy consequences for a student's education, safety and future, so they need a disciplined process rather than an improvised reaction. The book's position is that AI belongs only on the documentation side of that process, and only through tools the school has approved. Every decision in the process stays with people.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day use, a member of the threat assessment team might turn to an approved tool, one covered by a signed agreement, to organize notes or to draft a summary of how the team worked through its process. The text does not break this practice down by grade band, so the same boundary applies wherever a team operates. What the text rules out is putting any threat assessment information into a general chat tool, because those records are highly sensitive and may fall under strict legal rules. The team's own work, gathering evidence and conducting interviews, remains the source of its conclusions. The tool assists with the paperwork around that work and nothing more.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book cites research showing that people tend to go along with decisions a machine makes first, even poor ones (Krugel et al., 2023). That finding is the basis for its warning that a tool scoring a student's risk could anchor a team's judgment in ways that harm the student. The text gives no other study, figure or formal evidence label for this idea, so the case rests on that cited finding together with the practical judgment of the field. The recommendation that follows is that teams form their own views from evidence and interviews rather than from machine scores.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are strict. Threat assessment records are highly sensitive and may be subject to strict legal rules, so no such information should ever go into a general chat tool, and any tool used must be one the school has approved under a signed agreement. The deeper risk is that a machine's output can shape human judgment, and a risk score produced first could anchor a team in a direction that harms the student. The decisions themselves, the level of concern and the response, remain with people and cannot be handed to a machine. The team is responsible for reaching its own conclusions from evidence and interviews.
